raw_response:
I've been farming this 1.5 mu plot in Quzhou County for 15 years now. I'm 45, with an agricultural college background, and I know the technical recommendations inside out. But theory and practice diverge when you're working a plot this small. My wife and I handle the farm ourselves — our three children include two working off-farm in Shijiazhuang, sending remittances home. This land is mainly for our own grain security. We eat most of the wheat and sell the maize. My factory job limits my farming to evenings and weekends, so every decision has to balance agronomic sense against time and cash.

The maize in the field now will be hand-harvested by my wife and me in the first week of October — two days of work, no hired labor. It looks like a decent crop, maybe 450 kg/mu. I need to get the wheat in the ground by October 12–15 at the latest; the double-cropping window is tight but manageable at this scale. I'll do a quick rotary tillage after the maize comes off — no time for moldboard plowing.

For the winter wheat, I'm planting Jinmai 47, an improved semi-dwarf variety. I buy certified seed every few years, and this is the year: about 7.5 kg/mu at roughly 35 yuan/mu. On fertilizer, the county extension recommends 18 kg N/mu for a 500 kg/mu target, but I'm aiming for 400 kg/mu — realistic given my management constraints and the fact that I can't be out here every day. I'll broadcast 30 kg/mu of 15-15-15 compound before planting, giving me 4.5 kg each of N, P₂O₅, and K₂O per mu. At jointing in late March, I'll topdress 15 kg/mu of urea, which is another 6.9 kg N. Total N comes to about 11.5 kg/mu. I know I could push higher, but on 1.5 mu the marginal gain isn't worth diverting cash from household expenses. The phosphorus and potassium are modest but sufficient — I've managed this soil for 15 years and I know its baseline fertility.

Irrigation is non-negotiable for two timings: the winter irrigation before soil freeze-up to protect seedlings, and the jointing-stage irrigation in spring when water use efficiency is highest. That's two rounds at about 45 yuan/mu each with the electric pump. A third irrigation at grain-filling is a maybe — I'll watch the spring rainfall and my wallet. For pests, I'll spray herbicide once in early spring. I won't do routine fungicide; I walk this 1.5 mu every few days and can spot problems early.

For next summer's maize, I'll plant immediately after wheat harvest around June 12–15. With the tight turnaround, it'll be minimum tillage — maybe one quick rotary pass and plant the same day. Hybrid seed costs about 45 yuan/mu, but the yield advantage over local varieties is clear even on my small plot. I'll apply 25 kg/mu of compound at planting, then side-dress 20 kg/mu of urea at the 6–8 leaf stage. That gives about 13 kg N/mu total. Maize falls in the July–August rainy season, so I'm budgeting one irrigation in case of a mid-summer dry spell, but I often don't need it. Herbicide at planting or early post-emergence, and I'll monitor for corn borers.

Labor is all family: about 5 days across the wheat season and 4 for maize. No hired help — at 1.5 mu it makes no economic sense. My biggest worry is a dry spring at wheat jointing. If the rain doesn't come, I have to choose between a third irrigation or accepting yield loss. With my cash position, I'll probably accept some loss rather than spend more on pumping. That's the tradeoff of farming part-time.
